title: A Comprehensive Review of Autophagy and Its Various Roles in Infectious, Non-Infectious, and Lifestyle Diseases: Current Knowledge and Prospects for Disease Prevention, Novel Drug Design, and Therapy

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Concepts and Molecular Regulation of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Autophagy refers to the process of delivering cytoplasmic or extracellular components to the lysosomes of an animal cell or the vacuoles of plant or yeast cells. The production and maturation of autophagosomes are directly regulated by location, timing, and intensity. The phosphoinositide-binding protein, HS1BP3, is a negative regulator of autophagosome biogenesis that regulates the lipid composition and phosphatidic acid (PA) levels of autophagosome precursor membranes. Increased levels of systemic autophagy have been reported in Caenorhabditis

Liu and Levine described a novel form of non-apoptotic autophagic gene-dependent cell death, termed autosis, which is mediated by the Na + /K + -ATPase pump ref [14], ref [15]. Autosis involves enhanced cell-substrate adhesion, focal ballooning of the perinuclear space, and dilation and fragmentation of the endoplasmic reticulum ref [14]. The Tat-Beclin 1 peptide complex may initiate autosis, with the fusion of the evolutionarily conserved, 18-amino acid-long Beclin 1 domain with 11 amino acids from the HIV Tat protein transduction domain aiding the cellular entry of the fusion peptide ref [16]. The Tat-Beclin 1 fusion peptide has been shown to inhibit the replication of HIV, CHIKV, Sindbis (SINV), and WNV, as well as intracellular bacteria such as Listeria monocytogenes ref [13], ref [16], ref [17]. Tat-Beclin 1 treatment also reduced mortality in neonatal mice infected with CHIKV and WNV, demonstrated using a TUNEL assay, and cleared mutant Huntingtin protein aggregates ref [13], ref [16]. Autosis can be partially rescued by knocking down Atg13 or Atg14 or using 3-methyladenine. Under serum/amino acid starvation, approximately 1% of dying cells exhibit a morphology similar to that of cells treated with Tat-Beclin 1 and autosis is selectively blocked when the Na + /K + -ATPase pump is inhibited ref [14], ref [15]. During cerebral hypoxia or ischemia, the neonatal brain releases cardiac glycosides (ouabain or endobain), which inhibit the Na + /K + -ATPase pump and reduce autosis ref [15]. Autosis has also been observed in patients with severe liver anorexia nervosa who display focal ballooning of the perinuclear space, convoluted nucleus, dilated and fragmented ER, empty vacuoles, and several autolysosomes in their hepatocytes ref [14]. Ischemic injury can also lead to autosis in other organs, including the kidney and heart, which is attenuated in Beclin 1 +/− mice ref [15].

Several studies have documented interplay between autophagy and the NF-κB signaling pathway. Members of the NF-κB family of transcription factors regulate the transcription of genes involved in cell proliferation, survival, differentiation, and development, whilst activation of the inhibitor of NF-κB (IκBα) kinase complex is essential for autophagy induction. T-cell receptor-mediated NF-κB activation in B-cell lymphoma/leukemia is linked with the autophagy adaptor p62/SQSTM1 ref [20], which modulates the NLRP3-inflammasome activation and IL-1β production in macrophages.

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Concepts and Molecular Regulation of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Molecular Machinery of Autophagosome Biogenesis and Flux
subsections.content:
Macroautophagy is initiated when a portion of cytoplasm containing a cellular organelle is sequestered to form the autophagosome ref [9], ref [12]. The autophagosome fuses with the lysosome or late endosomal multivesicular bodies (MVBs) to degrade the materials within it ref [9], ref [11], ref [13]. Atg8 (microtubule-associated protein 1A/1B-light chain 3, LC3, is an Atg8 homolog in humans) was the first autophagosomal protein to be characterized ref [9], ref [13]. Macroautophagy can be classified as cargo-specific or non-selective ref [9], ref [13], ref [16].

Autophagy can promote or inhibit cell death depending on the cellular context; many other death mechanisms are intricately involved in the processes, with several mechanistic links elucidated between autophagy and other death mechanisms ref [9], ref [15].

IL-1α secretion is enhanced in Atg5-deficient macrophages, whilst inhibiting autophagy results in IL-1β overexpression. The anti-inflammatory cytokine, IL-10, inhibits autophagy by activating mTOR complex 1 ref [7], ref [10] and inhibits starvation-and IFN-γ-induced autophagy via Bcl-2 and Beclin 1 in various autoimmune and inflammatory disorders.

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Concepts and Molecular Regulation of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Signaling Networks and Molecular Regulation of Autophagy
subsections.content:
After the lysosome has formed vesicles by invaginating and engulfing small sections of the cytoplasm, lysosomal proteases degrade the contents of these vesicles. Microautophagy occurs during the biogenesis of multi-vesicular bodies (MVBs), which deliver soluble proteins to the late endosomes, and relies on electrostatic interactions between endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT) I and III and the heat-shock cognate protein 70 (HSC70). Hence, microautophagy involves both endocytic and autophagic components.

Autophagy and apoptosis regulation overlap when the BH3 domain of the Beclin 1 autophagy protein interacts with anti-apoptotic proteins of the Bcl-2 family, including Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, and Mcl-1 ref [19]. The BH3 domain has a critical role in the interaction between these proteins and has been shown to interact with the receptor domain of the Bcl-2 family in nutrient-rich cells ref [19]. Beclin 1-mediated autophagy is inhibited by ER-localized Bcl-2 ref [19]; the transgenic expression of Bcl-2 was shown to inhibit autophagy in mouse heart muscles. Beclin 1 mutants, which are unable to bind to Bcl-2, induce higher levels of autophagy than their wild-type counterparts ref [19]; hence the physical Beclin 1-Bcl-xL/Bcl-2 interaction regulates Beclin 1-mediated autophagy ref [19]. ABT737, a compound which mimics the BH3 domain and thus inhibits this interaction, increases the aggregation of LC3, an autophagy marker which is present on autophagosomes ref [19], in both nutrient-rich and nutrient-deprived media. Furthermore, the knockdown of Beclin 1 and other essential Atg proteins using siRNA heteroduplexes was shown to reduce ABT737-stimulated LC3 aggregation ref [19]. Atg12 is a dual-functioning protein that participates in both autophagy and apoptosis; non-conjugated Atg12 can bind and inhibit Mcl-1 and Bcl-2 via a BH3-like domain to positively regulate mitochondrial apoptosis. Atg12 knockout inhibits the release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria and apoptosis, whilst abnormal Atg12 expression represses the anti-apoptotic activity of Mcl-1.

Autophagy has predisposing, pathogenic, and therapeutic roles in autoimmunity ref [26]. Defects in autophagy pathways and/or autophagy-related genes have been implicated in numerous autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases, including multiple sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes mellitus, Crohn's disease, and vitiligo ref [26]. Abnormalities in the maintenance of homeostasis via autophagy result in the accumulation of dysfunctional or defective cellular organelles, abnormal proteins, infectious agents, and metabolite accumulation. This predisposes cells to the generation of autoantibodies and proinflammatory mediators and exposes vital and susceptible cellular structures to deleterious agents that can cause disease ref [26]. A recent study revealed a correlation between the expression pattern of autophagy-related genes and the type of lupus nephritis (LN); thus, autophagy could indicate of the type of LN when formulating a treatment regimen ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Concepts and Molecular Regulation of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Core Autophagy Pathways and Conceptual Framework
subsections.content:
Only proteins with a C-terminal pentapeptide KFERQ motif undergo CMA; the HSC70 cochaperone identifies cytosolic proteins containing this sequence and delivers them to the lysosome ref [27], ref [28], ref [37]. Chaperones bound to the substrate are transported to the lysosomal surface, where they interact with the monomeric LAMP-2A ref [27], ref [28], ref [37]. LAMP-2A must form a multiprotein complex to translocate the substrate ref [27], ref [28], ref [29], ref [37]; LAMP-2A complex assembly is a dynamic process that occurs when the substrate binds to the receptor ref [27], ref [28], ref [37]. The unfolded substrate protein (chaperon-mediated) is then translocated into the lysosome by LAMP-2A for degradation, following which LAMP-2A disassembles and its monomers are degraded in lipid microdomains ref [27], ref [28], ref [37]. The levels of LAMP-2A tightly regulate the rate of CMA at the lysosomal membrane ref [27], ref [28], ref [36], ref [37]. In the mammalian anti-viral defense system, a cell-autonomous autophagy mechanism has been identified wherein cellular p62 adaptormediated autophagic viral protein clearance induces cell survival ref [27], ref [28], ref [29]. Some positive-strand RNA viruses, including picornaviruses and influenza virus, promote autophagic membrane formation, and inhibit their final maturation (lysosomal fusion) ref [27], ref [28], ref [29]. Consequently, studying the interactions between autophagy and adenoviruses could improve adenoviral-based oncolytic virotherapies ref [27], ref [28], ref [29]. The process of CMA is depicted in Figure 2.

Necroptosis is often associated with inflammation ref [36]. The relationship between autophagy and necroptosis is complex, elusive, and slightly controversial since reports have indicated that necroptosis may promote, inhibit, or do not affect autophagy ref [27], ref [28], ref [29]. In several cell lines, including L929 cells, lymphocytes, and cancer cells, autophagy is activated in the presence of TNFα and under starvation to suppress necroptosis ref [27], ref [28], ref [36]. The apoptosis-inhibiting peptide, carbobenzoxy-Val-Ala-Asp (zVAD), prevents autophagy and induces necroptosis in response to TNFα by regulating lysosomal cathepsins, highlighting the pro-survival function of autophagy against necroptosis ref [27], ref [28]. Similarly, inhibiting the mTOR signaling pathway can prevent apoptosis and even enhance necroptosis, whereas starvation, which induces autophagy, protects cells from zVAD-mediated necroptotic death ref [27], ref [28], ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Concepts and Molecular Regulation of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy Crosstalk with Cell Death and Stress Adaptation
subsections.content:
Autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved process induced via multiple signaling pathways by numerous stimuli including nutrient starvation ref [16, 105] ref [39], hypoxia ref [82, 146] ref [39], oxidative stress ref [109, 147] ref [41], pathogen infection ref [39, 148] ref [41], and ER stress ref [149] ref [41]. In the presence of nutritional substances and cytokines, mechanistic/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) can prevent apoptosis and stimulate cell growth ref [150] ref [41], whereas stress and nutrient starvation inhibit mTOR to initiate autophagy via at least four molecular complexes, including the unc-51-like kinase (ULK) complex, consisting of ULK-1, Atg13, Atg101, and FAK-family interacting protein (FIP200); the PI3K complex, consisting of Atg15, vacuolar protein sorting (VPS)15, VPS34, Beclin 1, and Beclin 1-regulated autophagy protein 1 (AMBRA1) ref [151]ref [152]ref [153] ref [41]ref [5]; transmembrane protein complexes, including Atg9 and WIPI; and two ubiquitin-like protein conjugation systems (Atg12 and LC3) ref [154, 155] ref [41]ref [5].

Necrosis refers to the increase in cell volume caused by organelle swelling, which results in plasma membrane rupture and the loss of intracellular contents ref [41]ref [9]. When ATP is depleted, the cell is unable to undergo apoptosis and undergoes necrosis instead ref [201] ref [41]ref [9]. Poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP1) is an enzyme with roles in DNA repair, transcriptional regulation, and chromatin modification ref [202]. PARP1 over-activation decreases the ATP reservoir and induces necrotic cell death by bypassing energy-dependent apoptotic cell death ref [203] ref [41]ref [9]. ATP depletion also activates AMP-activated kinases (AMPK) ref [204], which induce autophagy by activating the ULK1 complex or inhibiting mTOR signaling ref [205] ref [41]ref [5]. Thus, DNA damage-induced PARP1 activation leads to a decline in ATP levels, AMPK activation, mTOR inhibition, and autophagy induction ref [206] ref [41]ref [5]. PARP1 plays a dual role in autophagy and necrosis since autophagy is a pro-survival mechanism, whilst necrosis is a pro-death mechanism ref [41]ref [9]. The fate of the cell depends on the balance between autophagy and necrosis, where autophagy represents the final attempt of the cell to survive before necrosis ref [38]ref [3]ref [4].

subsections.subsection_title: Host-Directed Modulation of Autophagy as an Anti-Infective Strategy
subsections.content:
Autophagy plays a beneficial role against infectious diseases by simultaneously degrading pathogens and activating the host immune system [ref 8, ref 14, ref 6]. This enables infections to be countered directly, by killing infectious agents, and indirectly, by inducing host immunity against pathogens [ref 8, ref 14]. Autophagy provides an excellent intracellular defense system against bacterial pathogens, including Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium [ref 3, ref 8], Listeria monocytogenes [ref 8, ref 14], and Shigella flexneri [ref 7, ref 8]. Anti-bacterial autophagy is termed xenophagy [ref 8, ref 14, ref 15]. Numerous cellular, membrane-associated, or cytoplasmic moieties modulate xenophagy [ref 8, ref 14, ref 6]; and those cells unable to carry out xenophagy, exhibit higher rates of infection [ref 8, ref 14]. Bcl-xL regulates xenophagy [ref 9, ref 15], and Bcl-xL knockout cells are more susceptible to Streptococcus pyogenes infection [ref 8]. The infection of non-phagocytic cells by Shigella flexneri is dependent upon type-III secretion system (T3SS) effector proteins [ref 7] which reorganize the host cell cytoskeleton, ruffle the cell membrane, and cause bacterial uptake [ref 7]. Following internalization, bacterial peptidoglycans are detected by nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD)-like receptors (NLRs) which trigger a pro-inflammatory immune response [ref 8, ref 14] (Figure 4). The bacteria-sensing NOD proteins interact with Atg16L1 to initiate anti-bacterial autophagosome biogenesis in response to bacterial invasion [ref 8, ref 14]. Intracellular bacterial sensing either by NLRs or sequestosome-1-like receptors (SLRs) recruits autophagy proteins, including unc-51-like kinase (ULK) 1/2 and lipid kinase complexed with Beclin 1 and Atg16L1, to initiate phagophore membrane nucleation and engulf invading bacteria [ref 6, ref 8, ref 14].

Various factors and mechanisms are involved in autophagy-mediated tumor progression [ref 16]. Tumor-induced nutrient shortage, cell debris (degraded proteins), inflammation, and oxidative cascades are all molecular mechanisms affecting tumor progression [ref 16, ref 9]. During nutrient starvation, autophagy induction promotes the survival of normal cells and may also promote tumor cell survival; however, hypoxia, metabolic stress, energy shortage, oxidative stress-damaged mitochondria, and organelles can be caused by cancer-causing genes or cancer treatments [ref 16, ref 9]. The undifferentiated colon cancer cell line, HT-29, and other transformed cells have shown an increased tendency to degrade autophagic proteins [ref 16]. The elevated expression of the autophagy signature protein, BNIP3, a pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 member, has been demonstrated in colorectal and gastric epithelial carcinomas, suggesting that BNIP3 expression may be important for the development of these cancers [ref 16]. The activation of autophagy and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) was shown to protect colon cancer cells against apoptosis induced by the interaction between butyrate and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) in a cell type-dependent manner [ref 16]. Additionally, an Atg8/LC3 family member implicated in autophagy and tumor suppression was associated with alterations to cell death and cytokine secretion in mice lacking gamma-aminobutyric acid receptor-associated protein (GABARAP) [ref 16]. It has been well documented that inhibiting autophagy in cancer cells increases their death, with this strategy proving most useful in tumors that behave like RAS-activated tumors [ref 16, ref 9]. Inhibiting autophagy is expected to cause ubiquitinated proteins to accumulate and p62 levels to increase; in hepatic tumors, autophagy suppresses spontaneous tumorigenesis via cell-intrinsic pathways whilst p62 accumulation promotes tumor formation [ref 19, ref 16, ref 18, ref 20].

Iron homeostasis involves a form of macroautophagy known as ferritinophagy, wherein ferritin, an iron storage protein, is degraded in the lysosome [ref 15, ref 6]. Iron levels are tightly regulated in cells; nutrient deficiency induces autophagy, during which cellular proteins and organelles are engulfed by the autophagosome, which then fuses with the lysosome [ref 6, ref 15]. The degradation of these contents provides essential resources that either promote cell survival or lead to cell death [ref 6, ref 9]. Iron (Fe), copper (Cu), zinc (Zn), and aluminum (Al) react with molecular oxygen to produce reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS). Besides acting as a cofactor for metalloprotein enzymes involved in redox reactions, iron also plays a major role in mitochondrial ATP metabolism and other cellular processes. The Fenton and Haber-Weiss redox reaction is highly involved in ROS production and Alzheimer's progression [ref 15]. To maintain iron homeostasis, storage and recycling are critical [ref 15, ref 6]. When engulfed by macrophages, the iron within erythrocytes is either stored as a ferritin complex or exported from the cell by the ferroportin iron-exporter [ref 15].

subsections.subsection_title: Pathogen Subversion of Autophagy for Intracellular Survival
subsections.content:
Autophagy has a beneficial role in cellular defense against invasion by viruses; therefore, it has been used for antiviral immunity ref [141, 233, 234]. Autophagy helps to clear viral pathogens during infection via various molecular mechanisms, regulates immune responses, and prevents harmful overactivation and inflammation ref [235]. For example, autophagy increases the presentation of endogenous viral antigens in the peptide grooves of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules on the cell surface during herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection. Studies of viral peptides have suggested a complex interaction between vacuoles and MHC class I presentation pathways in autophagosomes ref [236]. In contrast, MHC class II molecules continuously accept input from autophagosomes, which facilitates antigen presentation by MHC class II molecules ref [237, 238]. Autophagy is a major component of Drosophila immunity against vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) ref [239] as it can deliver viral antigens to TLRs for presentation. During anti-viral signaling, pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) at the plasma membrane (i.e., Toll-7) that are engaged by VSV stimulate an autophagy-dependent innate immune response mediated by PI3K-Akt-signaling ref [239, 240]. Furthermore, Toll/TLR signaling has been shown to regulate the Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV) replication in both flies and mammals ref [241], whilst SIRT1, an NAD(+)-dependent deacetylase, modulates the activation of dendritic cells and autophagy during induced immune responses against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) ref [242], thereby directing an effective anti-viral immune response. Furthermore, autophagy is stimulated by the salicylamide derivatives against cytopathic bovine viral diarrhea virus (cp-BVDV), a Flaviviridae pestivirus ref [243]. Foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) infection suppresses autophagy and NF-κB anti-viral activities by degrading Atg5-Atg12 using the viral protein, 3C pro, suggesting that Atg5-Atg12 positively modulates anti-viral NF-κB and IRF3 pathways during FMDV infection to limit FMDV proliferation ref [244]. However, autophagy is often hijacked by viral pathogens and can be modulated to their own benefit (ref [8], ref [9], ref [10], ref [11]).

There is growing evidence that autophagy performs both physiological and pathological functions in the nervous system, and that autophagic stimulation plays critical roles in neuronal survival and activity (ref [12]). Autophagy is the only method by which neurons degrade and excrete expired organelles, and is responsible for clearing abnormal intracytoplasmic contents from normal cells which would otherwise cause protein accumulation and damage neuronal activity, inducing severe functional impairment (ref [12]). Autophagy also clears protein aggregates from old neurons; thus, inhibiting autophagy can lead to neuronal degeneration and intraneuronal protein accumulation (ref [12]). Mutations in Atg5 confined to neural tissues can cause impaired growth, progressive motor and behavioral deficits, prominent neurodegeneration, and axonal swelling in regions of the brain with increased levels of ubiquitinylated proteins, indicating that autophagy has a neuroprotective role ref [319]. In mammals, the absence of Atg59 and Atg710 can cause severe neurodegeneration, further supporting the neuroprotective role of autophagy ref [100, 320]. Furthermore, neuronal death can be attributed to the loss of basal autophagy or an imbalance in autophagic flux. In some neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's, as well as in the brain or spinal cord trauma, the damaged neurons exhibit abnormally high numbers of autophagosomes. Therefore, understanding the interaction between pathophysiological mechanisms and autophagy could be a promising approach for therapies against neurological disorders ref [321]. Prenatal alcohol exposure has been shown to increase the number of autophagic vacuoles in the cortical micro-vessels of human fetal and mouse neonatal brains, impairing autophagy ref [322]. Furthermore, autophagy can modulate Notch degradation, stem cell development, and neurogenesis ref [323].

Autophagy is involved in obesity ref [388] and diabetes mellitus ref [389]. Improper lipid and glycogen processing can affect the liver activity and thus, insulin synthesis, resulting in diabetes. Studies have shown that hepatocytes from mouse models of obesity display reduced autophagy ref [390], with decreased Atg7 expression causing ER stress and affecting insulin signaling ref [390]. Mutant Atg7 mice also exhibit reduced β cell mass, reduced insulin circulation, and glucose intolerance, indicating that autophagy defects can reduce insulin levels and cause hyperglycemia ref [391, 392]. A genetic mosaic screen for mutations that increase lysosomal and/or autophagic activity in D. melanogaster larva revealed that autophagy-lysosome pathways underlie novel cytoprotective features in Drosophila ref [393]. Obesity impairs autophagy in the liver via S-nitrosylation, a process induced by nitric oxide (NO). S-nitrosylation of the lysosomal enzymes cathepsin B (CTSB) and hexosaminidase subunit β (HexB) impairs normal lysosomal functioning and is carried out by denitrosylation enzymes, particularly S-nitrosoglutathione reductase (GSNOR) and thioredoxin ref [394]. Obesity inhibits the denitrosylation ability of the liver, impairing hepatic autophagy and insulin resistance ref [395]. In obese animals, hepatic insulin signaling is impaired by NO-induced hepatic autophagy repression, which ultimately causes the progression of type 2 diabetes ref [396].

subsections.subsection_title: Xenophagy as a Cell-Autonomous Antibacterial Defense
subsections.content:
Subverting the autophagic pathway can have adverse consequences by giving pathogens access to nutrients for growth and reproduction ref [69], ref [75]. Autophagy plays an important role in viral replication and pathogenesis ref [69], with coronaviruses, coxsackievirus B3, poliovirus, hepatitis C virus (HCV), and DENV all known to stimulate and require autophagy for accelerated replication, whereas infectious bursal disease virus and hepatitis B virus also exploit or induce autophagy to promote stages of their life cycle ref [79], ref [80]. For instance, autophagy has been demonstrated to be actively involved in the replication of influenza A virus (IAV), which induces autophagosome formation during the early phase of infection and later inhibits autophagosomal maturation by preventing autophagosomal-lysosomal fusion and promoting autophagosomes to accumulate in virus-infected cells. Autophagy-deficient cells are more susceptible to apoptosis upon influenza infection, while using pharmacological reagents or RNA interference to alter cellular autophagy can impair viral protein accumulation. Human single-chain antibody variable fragments (ScFvs) which bind to the influenza A virus ion channel protein (M2) and inhibit viral replication were found to restore autophagosome maturation suppressed by the infecting virus (personal communication). It has also been reported that HCV can trigger autophagy via immunity-related GTPase M, which promotes HCV replication. Paramyxoviruses such as Newcastle disease virus (NDV) have been shown to trigger autophagy in U251 glioma cells to enhance viral replication. In addition, modulating NDV-induced autophagy using rapamycin, chloroquine, or small interfering RNAs which target genes critical for autophagosome formation (Atg5 and Beclin 1) affects virus production, suggesting that NDV may utilize autophagy to promote its replication. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) uses multiple methods to regulate autophagy and enhance its replication ref [69]. HIV induces the early stages of autophagy but inhibits the later stages which would suppress the production of new virions. The HIV-1 accessory protein, Nef, inhibits autophagosomal maturation by interacting with Beclin 1, whilst the HIV protein Vpr can trigger autophagy in transfected THP-1 macrophages, indicating that autophagy may be involved in maintaining HIV reservoirs in macrophages. HSV-1, Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), and mouse herpesvirus 68 (MHV-68) encode proteins that bind Beclin 1 to prevent autophagy initiation ref [69].

Several reviews have evaluated the relationship between autophagy and neurodegenerative diseases. Autophagy is vital for neuronal homeostasis. Autophagy is also a cell-autonomous antibacterial defense pathway that recognizes and restricts intracellular microbes ref [69], ref [70], ref [73], ref [75]. Its deregulation is highly associated with host susceptibility to infection and bacterial persistence, including the accumulation of intracellular pathogens or damaged vacuoles with pathological consequences in infections caused by Salmonella, Shigella, Listeria, streptococci, and mycobacteria ref [70], ref [71], ref [72], ref [76], ref [77], ref [78]. Lysosomal system inactivation is responsible for the accumulation of autophagosomes observed during impaired antibacterial clearance, whilst defective autophagosomal degradation or blocked fusion can favor pathogen survival ref [69], ref [75], ref [78]. Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium is a key example where autophagosomal targeting and anomalies in the endosomal-lysosomal pathway have been observed after vacuolar damage, enabling xenophagic recognition in damaged vacuoles ref [70], ref [73]. Listeria monocytogenes is another key example, where bacterial determinants such as ActA help evade autophagic recognition and where noncanonical autophagy may occur upon phagocytosis before growth-restricting xenophagy is avoided ref [71], ref [77]. Shigella flexneri interactions with the autophagy machinery further illustrate how pathogens can be selectively recognized yet actively subvert or escape xenophagy ref [72], ref [75]. Autophagy deficiency resulted in impaired antibacterial defense in model systems, and autophagy genes protect against Salmonella typhimurium infection and mediate pathogen resistance ref [73]. In addition, HLH-30/TFEB-mediated autophagy functions in a cell-autonomous manner for epithelium intrinsic cellular defense against bacterial pore-forming toxin in C. elegans ref [74]. Dysfunction or abnormalities in autophagy, including blockade of autophagosome-lysosome fusion by bacterial or host factors, are accompanied by enhanced intracellular survival of pathogens with exceptional frequency ref [69], ref [75], ref [78]. Group A Streptococcus-induced autophagy is one example in which Bcl-xL affects the process directly by inhibiting fusion between autophagosomes and lysosomes, and indirectly by inhibiting bacterial internalization via interaction with Beclin 1-UVRAG ref [78]. Autophagy is also an innate mechanism associated with leprosy polarization, further supporting its importance in antibacterial immunity in human disease ref [76].

subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Antiviral Immunity and Viral Pathogenesis
subsections.content:
Initially, autophagy was thought to be involved in tumor suppression by stimulating gene expression, inhibiting proinflammatory mediators, inhibiting inflammation or inflammatory products, and stimulating signaling pathways ref [81]. The essential Atg6/Beclin 1 gene was found to be important in virus–host interactions and antiviral protection ref [5], whereas excessive autophagy stimulation by Beclin 1 overexpression has been reported to inhibit virus-associated pathogenic progression in some models ref [5], ref [81]. Autophagy modulates inflammation and inflammatory products during infection, including innate antiviral immunity ref [81], ref [88], ref [89]. In cell-based assays, inhibiting autophagy was shown to enhance or suppress viral growth depending on the virus studied ref [85], ref [89], ref [90]. p62 (a signaling adaptor/scaffold protein) is involved in the formation of intracellular ubiquitin-related protein aggregates because of autophagy deficiency ref [81]. Atg7-deficient settings exhibit altered autophagic processing and cargo handling in infected cells ref [81], ref [83]. Autophagy has also been implicated in virus-induced membrane remodeling ref [84], and the inactivation of Beclin 1 and Atg5 was shown to alter susceptibility to viral disease in experimental systems ref [5], ref [81]. Atg5-and Atg7-deficient conditions exhibited defective autophagic responses, indicating that impaired autophagy can affect host defense and disease outcome ref [81], ref [83]. Heterozygous Beclin 1 was shown to have altered susceptibility to infection-associated pathology ref [5], whilst Beclin 1 inhibited pathogenic progression in infected cell systems ref [5], ref [81]. The UVRAG protein was found to participate in autophagosome maturation pathways that can be targeted during viral infection ref [81], ref [94] (Figure 6). cancer in mice ref [292]. Atg5-and Atg7-deficient mice exhibited liver tumors, indicating that defective autophagy can affect the suppression of tumorigenesis ref [292]. Heterozygous Beclin 1 (beclin 1+/mutant) was shown to have a high incidence of spontaneous tumors ref [289, 293], whilst Beclin 1 inhibited tumor growth in cell lines such as the breast cancer cell line, MCF-7, in which Beclin 1 expression was lower than in normal epithelial breast cells ref [294]. The UVRAG protein was found to suppress the tumorigenicity and proliferation of human colonic cancer cells ref [295] (Figure 6). ref [4] mTOR is implicated in cancer and its substrates include the eukaryotic initiation factor 4E (eIF4E)-binding proteins (4E-BPs) and the ribosomal S6 kinases (S6Ks) 1 and 2, which promote cell cycle progression. The mTOR, which is inhibited by rapamycin, induces autophagy ref [81], ref [87], ref [96], ref [98]. ref [5] A novel anti-cancer molecule, HA15, which targets HSPA5/BIP was shown to induce endoplasmic reticulum stress and increase the unfolded protein response, resulting in cancer cell death through autophagy and apoptosis ref [87], ref [88].

Under normal conditions, the myocardium exhibits low levels of autophagy, whilst stressful conditions can increase the level of autophagy to increase cell survival ref [81]. Patients with congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease, hypertension, and aortic valvular disease display increased autophagosomal accumulation in their myocardial biopsies ref [368]. Autophagy levels vary in normal and affected or stressed hearts, with constitutive autophagy maintaining normal structure and function, and upregulated autophagy occurring during cardiac disease or stress ref [369]. In Atg5-deficient mice, contractile dysfunction and hypertrophy have been observed during cardiomyopathy ref [370], whilst cell culture studies have revealed that autophagic gene deficiency can cause the accumulation of unwanted proteins and contribute to myocardial disease ref [371]. Similarly, LAMP-2-deficient mice displayed increased autophagic vacuole accumulation and could not degrade proteins, thereby promoting cardiomyopathy ref [371, 372]. It has been postulated that during early life, between birth and suckling, autophagy provides the energy required for cardiac cells ref [373], whilst mitophagy protects cardiac muscles under ischemic stress ref [374]. In antiviral immunity, autophagy contributes to antigen processing and presentation, including major histocompatibility complex class II-restricted presentation of cytosolic antigens ref [82]. It also regulates immune-cell activation during respiratory viral infection, as shown for dendritic-cell activation and autophagy during respiratory syncytial virus-induced immune responses ref [83]. Conversely, many viruses subvert autophagy to favor replication or persistence ref [81]. Hepatitis C virus proteins induce distinct membrane alterations including candidate viral replication complexes ref [84], and hepatitis C virus induces an incomplete autophagic response via the unfolded protein response ref [87]. Activation of the unfolded protein response and autophagy after hepatitis C virus infection suppresses innate antiviral immunity in vitro ref [88], whereas knockdown of autophagy enhances the innate immune response in hepatitis C virus-infected hepatocytes ref [89] and inhibits infectious hepatitis C virus release by the exosomal pathway ref [99]. Autophagosomes support coxsackievirus B3 replication in host cells ref [85], and poliovirus modifies the cellular autophagy protein LC3 ref [86]. Autophagy is involved in influenza A virus replication ref [90]. Human immunodeficiency virus type-1 infection inhibits autophagy ref [91], yet the autophagy pathway also intersects with HIV-1 biosynthesis and regulates viral yields in macrophages ref [92], and HIV-1 Nef dysregulates autophagy in human astrocytes ref [93]. Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus K7 modulates Rubicon-mediated inhibition of autophagosome maturation ref [94], and γ-herpesvirus 68 encodes Bcl-2-mediated down-regulation of autophagy ref [95]. Flavivirus NS4A-induced autophagy protects cells against death and enhances virus replication ref [96]. Autophagy is also involved in coronavirus replication ref [97], and coronavirus Nsp6 proteins generate autophagosomes from the endoplasmic reticulum via an omegasome intermediate ref [98]. Protection against fatal Sindbis virus encephalitis by beclin further highlights a direct antiviral and disease-limiting role for autophagy machinery ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Genetic Disorders and Disease States Associated with Autophagy Dysfunction
subsections.subsection_title: Muscle and Renal Inflammatory/Degenerative Disease States
subsections.content:
Maintaining homeostasis is the most important role of autophagy, which is the final survival mechanism used to escape cell death. Mutations or genetic dysfunctions in autophagy-associated genes can have a variety of pathological consequences, as described below: ref [100], ref [101], ref [102], ref [103]

To alleviate autophagy-associated diseases, a variety of drugs, biomolecules, chemicals, and epigenetic strategies have been developed to either promote or inhibit autophagy. ref [104], ref [107], ref [109], ref [112], ref [113], ref [114], ref [115], ref [116], ref [117], ref [118], ref [119]

Lysosomal proteases are active at an acidic pH. The protease inhibitor leupeptin inhibits cysteine, serine, and threonine peptidases to block protein degradation and thus inhibits the final step of autophagy, as evidenced by the accumulation of vacuolar autolysosomes ref [105]. Cathepsins are aspartic, cysteine, and serine proteases that are transported to lysosomes via mannose-6-phosphate receptors and can be inhibited by the lysosomal protease inhibitors E64d and pepstatin A. Cells treated with E64d and pepstatin A exhibit increased LC3-II levels ref [108].

Lithium chloride (LiCl) can induce autophagy by inhibiting inositol monophosphatase (IMPase), which reduces inositol and inositol-1,4,5-triphosphate (IP3) levels. Since lithium has already been approved by the FDA for patients with bipolar disorder, it can easily be adapted for other diseases. Long-term oral lithium administration enhanced autophagy in a tauopathy mouse model by inhibiting glycogen synthase kinase-3 ref [112]. L-690,330, a bisphosphonate inhibitor of IMPase, exhibits a similar function to lithium by clearing mutant synucleins and EGFP-HDQ74 ref [106]. Valproic acid is an angio-suppressive compound which suppresses the Akt/mTOR signaling pathway by acting as a histone deacetylase inhibitor and promotes autophagy, as evidenced by the increased concentrations of LC3-II and Beclin 1 after its administration in prostate cancer cell lines ref [110], ref [111], ref [113]. Carbamazepine and valproic acid can both reduce intracellular inositol-1,4,5 trisphosphate levels. Therefore, other IMPase inhibitors could also be incorporated into therapeutic strategies ref [115], ref [116], ref [117], ref [118], ref [119].

subsections.section_title: Genetic Disorders and Disease States Associated with Autophagy Dysfunction
subsections.subsection_title: Crohn's Disease and Inflammatory Bowel Disease
subsections.content:
Crohn's disease is a major inflammatory bowel disease whose symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and weight loss ref [120] ref [122]. Atg16L1 mutations have been found to be linked with Crohn's disease ref [120] ref [122]. Atg16L1 forms a complex with Atg12-Atg5 which initiates autophagosome formation by inducing the conjugation of LC3 with PE ref [121] ref [122]. A study on the 300T > A Atg16L1 mutation revealed that the mutation is differentially involved in Crohn's disease and canonical autophagy ref [121] ref [123]. In mice, the mutations that eliminated or reduced Atg16L1 expression indicated a relationship between Atg16L1 mutations and Crohn's disease ref [120] ref [122]. Other autophagy-associated proteins, including IRGM-101, 102, and 103 and NOD2-104, 105, and 106 have also been linked to Crohn's disease in humans ref [120] ref [122]. Autophagy is thought to be involved in the pathogenesis of Crohn's disease, but it can also control disease severity by reducing the levels of inflammatory mediators ref [120] ref [122].

Autophagy can be suppressed during any stage of autophagic flux ref [126]. The pro-apoptotic role of autophagy may lead to hyperstimulation-induced excessive activation, which results in detrimental self-cannibalism that can go beyond the limit of cellular recovery ref [126] ref [127]. Numerous chemical inhibitors have been identified and tested in various cell and animal models ref [124] ref [126]. Most autophagy inhibitors are poorly selective, limiting their wider applications ref [126].

The Atg genes are crucial in autophagy; therefore, the inactivation or knockdown of these genes may be a useful way to manipulate the process ref [124] ref [126]. MiR-30a has been reported to downregulate Beclin 1 and Atg5 expression, whilst miR-101 can inhibit basal and rapamycin-induced autophagy ref [126]. Autophagy is induced by the activation of the ULK complex, which consists of ULK1/2, Atg13, FIP200, and Atg101 ref [126]. In melanoma cells, miR-290-295 clusters can inhibit ULK1 and Atg7 expression to suppress autophagic cell death ref [126]. MiR-885-3p targets ULK2 to regulate autophagy ref [126], whereas miRNA-30a/b, miRNA-376b, miR-216a, miR-519a, and miR-17-5p inhibit Beclin 1 expression to suppress vesicle nucleation ref [126]. Recently, the leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 gene (LRRK2), which is associated with Crohn's disease, Parkinson's disease, and leprosy, was shown to inhibit the non-canonical autophagy cascade, indicating that the negative regulation of this cascade could directly induce disease ref [120] ref [122]. In addition, the Atg16L1 300 T > A polymorphism has been demonstrated to disrupt unconventional TMEM59.110-mediated autophagy in mice ref [123].

Anacardic acid, curcumin, garcinol, and spermidine increase autophagy by reducing the level of acetylation in cultured human cells, as evidenced by depleted sequestosome-1 levels and mTORC1 inhibition ref [125]. Spermidine also inhibits EP300 and the major autophagy proteins, Atg5, Atg7, Atg12, and LC3 to repress autophagy ref [125] ref [126]. Supplementing the diet of mice with coffee beans rich in polyphenols concomitantly increased autophagy and decreased acetylation levels ref [125], whilst natural polyamines can inhibit acetyltransferases, and their dietary intake can improve the life span of short-living mouse strains and the health of long-living ones ref [125].

subsections.section_title: Genetic Disorders and Disease States Associated with Autophagy Dysfunction
subsections.content:
HSP is a neurodegenerative disorder that causes axonal degeneration in the corticospinal or pyramidal motor and sensory tracts that control distal organs and is caused by a recessive mutation in the TECPR2 gene. TECPR2 interacts with six human Atg8 orthologs to positively regulate autophagy, with TECPR2 knockdown in HeLa cells reducing autophagic activity and indicating its role in autophagy. The zinc-finger protein spastizin interacts with the Beclin 1-UVRAG-Rubicon complex and is involved in autophagosome maturation. In fibroblasts derived from patients with HSP, knockout of the spastizin gene reduced autophagy and caused autophagosome accumulation by impairing lysosomal fusion ref [129]. The ZFYVE26/SPASTIZIN and SPG11/SPATACSIN mutations were recently associated with HSP ref [130]; however, there are currently no treatments available to reverse nerve degeneration in HSP, with efforts instead directed towards reducing symptoms by physiotherapy and improving spasticity using medication.

3-methyladenine (3-MA), a class-III PI3K inhibitor, is commonly used to inhibit autophagy. Class III PI3K and Beclin 1 are essential during the first step of autophagy induction; thus, inhibiting PI3K reduces autophagosome formation. Bafilomycin A1 is a vacuolar H + -ATPase inhibitor, which functions at concentrations as low as 1 nM to inhibit both the early and late stages of autophagy by activating the mTOR pathway. In early 1998, bafilomycin A1 was reported to inhibit autophagic vacuoles in rat hepatoma by dissociating the Beclin 1-Vps34 complex and preventing autolysosome formation, thus attenuating functional autophagy. Bafilomycin A1 has been tested in a mouse model and found to be safe. Furthermore, disruption of the vacuolar-type H + -ATPase complex in mouse liver cells has been shown to induce the rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1)-independent aggravation of autophagic vacuoles and lysosomes. Concanamycin A belongs to the same class of vacuolar H + -ATPase inhibitors as bafilomycin A1 and in the presence of autophagosomes causes autophagic bodies to accumulate in the central vacuole and cytoplasm of tobacco BY-2 cells. Therefore, vacuolar-type H + -ATPases have been proposed as potential therapeutic agents.

Rapamycin, also known as sirolimus, is a natural mTOR inhibitor that stimulates autophagy both in vitro and in vivo; however, its long-term use is often complicated as it suppresses ribosome biogenesis and protein translation ref [131]. The rapamycin ester CCI-779/Temsilorimus, which is also an mTOR inhibitor, prevents the development of intracellular tau protein inclusions (abundant protein that stabilizes microtubules in CNS neurons) which are known to accumulate in neurons in Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies and can also reduce the density of neurofibrillary tangles by stimulating mTOR-dependent autophagy ref [131]. RAD001 and AP23573 are rapamycin derivatives with comparatively high safety and low toxicity ref [131]. During the early stages of carotid atherosclerosis, which is an inflammatory step in the primary pathogenesis of cerebrovascular diseases, miRNA-155 plays an important role in the activation of autophagy by rapamycin. Rapamycin has also been shown to increase autophagy, decrease cyclin D1 expression, and attenuate aggressive IgA nephropathy progression in a rat model.

Fluoxetine, which selectively improves the secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF-α, and gefitinib, which inhibits the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), can also enhance autophagy to impart neuroprotection and restrict M. tuberculosis growth ref [9]. The antiepileptic compound, carbamazepine, has been found to protect cells against M. tuberculosis infection, likely by inducing autophagy ref [9]. Elevated intracytosolic Ca 2+ levels can inhibit autophagy; penitrem A, which inhibits Ca 2+ -dependent K + channels, is known to induce autophagy and has been used to treat neurodegenerative disorders. Furthermore, bacterial pore-forming toxins can induce the expression of the transcription factor HLH-30 (TFEB) in C. elegans, which stimulates autophagy genes and thus inhibits bacterial infection ref [8]. Metformin, an AMPK activator, has been shown to induce autophagy and reduce the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in diabetic patients.

subsections.section_title: Genetic Disorders and Disease States Associated with Autophagy Dysfunction
subsections.content:
Danon disease is a rare cardiomyopathic disease caused by LAMP-2 deficiency and characterized by the accumulation of glycogen and autophagic vacuoles in cardiac and skeletal muscles, cardiomyopathy, and intellectual dysfunction ref [435] ref [135]. The LAMP-2 gene is alternatively spliced into three isoforms (LAMP-2A, -2B, and -2C) which have different functions in autophagy ref [135]. LAMP-2A acts as a receptor for CMA, in which proteins carrying the KFERQ motif are selectively trafficked into the lysosome and degraded ref [133]. LAMP-2B has been suggested to play a prominent role in macroautophagy and is responsible for the Danon phenotype ref [135]. LAMP-2B-deficient mice exhibit higher mortality and autophagic vacuole accumulation in the liver, kidney, pancreas, and cardiac and skeletal muscles ref [372] ref [133]. Whole genome sequencing identified a nonsense mutation (codon 520C>T in exon 4) in LAMP2 in a family with Danon disease ref [436] ref [134]. LAMP-2 knockout resulted in failed autophagic progression, as evidenced by inappropriate cathepsin D processing in the autophagic vacuoles and abnormally high numbers of mannose-6-phosphate receptors that limited the degradation of long-lived proteins during starvation ref [437] ref [135].

Cycloheximide is a protein biosynthesis inhibitor that is frequently used in biomedical research. In mouse pancreatic acinar cells, cadmium chloride-or hyperosmotic sucrose-stimulated autophagy was found to be inhibited by cycloheximide ref [467], which likely inhibits autophagy at the segregation step. Cycloheximide is used to prevent the autophagy-lysosome pathway ref [468] and its effects can be rapidly reversed by its removal ref [469].

The immunosuppressive activities of rapamycin limit its frequent use; therefore, safer molecules are required. Three SMERs were identified from 50,729 compounds that can induce autophagy ref [492]; SMERs 10, 18, and 28 can reduce the pathogenesis associated with polyglutamine aggregation and A53T α-synuclein, which are linked to Huntington's disease and familial Parkinson's disease, respectively ref [493], and induce autophagy in an mTOR-independent manner ref [141]. In addition, the small molecule AUTEN-99 activates autophagy in cell cultures and animal models and inhibits the progression of neurodegenerative symptoms ref [343].

subsections.section_title: Genetic Disorders and Disease States Associated with Autophagy Dysfunction
subsections.subsection_title: Cancer and Other Pathologic States Involving Autophagy Dysregulation
subsections.content:
sIBM is an age-related progressive muscle disorder which presents in the elderly and is characterized by the presence of autophagic vacuoles and ubiquitinylated misfolded multiprotein aggregates ref [10]. Two major lysosomal proteases, cathepsins D and B, exhibit decreased activation in sIBM muscle fibers ref [145] whilst LC3-II is increased, indicating that autophagosome formation is increased due to reduced cathepsin D and B activity during autophagosome maturation ref [145]. T cells may have a role in sIBM, whilst allelic variants of the HLA-DR3 locus, other genetic factors, and the HLA genotype are also thought to play major roles in the progression and severity of the disease.

Chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, NH 4 Cl, and neutral red are chemicals that can rapidly neutralize the acidic environment of the lysosome; therefore, they are used to block autophagosome maturation ref [143]. Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are repurposed drugs that have been used to treat malaria, SLE, and rheumatoid arthritis; however, higher hydroxychloroquine concentrations are required to induce active autophagy as a cancer treatment, which are usually not achievable in cancer patients ref [142]. Chloroquine-mediated lysosomal dysfunction is thought to have increased anti-cancer functions when combined with nutrient deprivation ref [142]. Lys01, a dimeric form of chloroquine in which each molecule is separated by the spacer molecule N-bis(2-aminoethyl)-methylamine, has been reported to inhibit autophagy at a level 10-fold higher than chloroquine. Lys05, a water-soluble salt of Lys01, effectively accumulates within the lysosome to concurrently deacidify and inhibit autophagy ref [142], ref [143].

Trehalose is a natural disaccharide known to stimulate autophagy via AMPK ref [10]. In cultured cells from an animal model of Huntington's disease, trehalose has been shown to stimulate autophagy and reduce Huntingtin protein aggregation during starvation by inhibiting a family of glucose transporters known as the solute carrier 2 or the glucose transporter family ref [10]. As well as being an autophagy activator and a non-reducing disaccharide, trehalose can also reduce the levels of aggregate-prone proteins and ameliorate cytotoxicity in neurodegenerative disease models ref [10]. Trehalose treatment has been shown to increase the conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II via an mTOR-independent pathway, whilst sucrose and raffinose are also known to induce autophagy ref [10]. It has been shown that trehalose can be used to safely induce autophagy in neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's disease ref [10], Alzheimer's disease ref [10], and prion disease ref [10]. The bioavailability of trehalose in the body for autophagy induction is low due to the hydrolytic enzyme, trehalase, which is expressed in the intestine and kidney; therefore, the enzyme-stable trehalose analogs, lentztrehaloses A, B, and C, were synthesized and found to be as effective as trehalose ref [10].

Compounds that inhibit and activate autophagy. Autophagy inhibitors: 3-methyladenine inhibits PI3K ref [451]. Bafilomycin A1 causes dissociation of the Beclin 1-Vps34 complex and prevents the formation of autolysosome ref [453]. Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine, NH 4 Cl, and leupeptin rapidly neutralizing the acidic environment of the lysosome and are used to block lysosomal degradation of substrates ref [454], ref [455], ref [456]. Leupeptin inhibits cysteine, serine and threonine peptidases, and hence blocking protein degradation at the last step of autophagy ref [457]. Autophagy activators: rapamycin inhibits the mTOR ref [458]. RAD001 and AP23573 are rapamycin derivatives having comparatively higher safely with minimum dose toxicities ref [459], ref [460]. Trehalose causes LC3-I to LC3-II conversion in an mTOR-independent pathway ref [461]. Valproic acid increases LC3-II and Beclin 1 concentrations ref [462].

Autophagy is a fast-moving area of science which has had an excellent positive impact on animal and human health-related issues and threatening diseases and has considerable future potential ref [463], ref [464]. Autophagy is a highly complex process, and understanding the complexity of its mechanisms and internal regulations will be highly beneficial for developing novel methods such as simple ameba-based experimental models ref [465], ref [466]. Emerging studies have established many interesting connections in the field of autophagy research ref [467], ref [468]. Since autophagy is one of the most conserved evolutionary processes, present in lower organisms and all highly evolved mammals, much work has been carried out to understand its physiological and pathological features ref [469], ref [470], ref [471]. Pathogenesis-associated autophagy is involved in degenerative, inflammatory, infectious, and neoplastic diseases ref [472], ref [473], ref [474], ref [475], ref [476], ref [477], ref [478], ref [479], whereas physiological autophagy is associated with maintaining liver iron homeostasis, CNS development, endothelial cell alignment, atheroprotection, and preventing infection ref [480], ref [481], ref [482], ref [483], ref [484], ref [485], ref [486], ref [487], ref [488], ref [489], ref [490], ref [491].
